## Quiz time {#dd-quiz}

**Raise your hand if you have already used:**

::: {.incremental}
- **VHDL**

- **Verilog or SystemVerilog**

- an **FPGA**

- an **ASIC design flow**
:::

## Two languages, one multiplier {#dd-hdl}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
**VHDL**

```vhdl
library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

entity mul4 is
  port(a, b : in  unsigned(3 downto 0);
       p    : out unsigned(7 downto 0));
end entity;

architecture rtl of mul4 is
begin
  p <= a * b;
end architecture;
```
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
**SystemVerilog**

```systemverilog
module mul4(
  input  logic [3:0] a, b,
  output logic [7:0] p
);
  assign p = a * b;
endmodule
```

::: {.fragment}
Both describe the same **4-bit × 4-bit combinational behavior**. Synthesis
chooses its concrete implementation.
:::
:::
::::

## Combinational logic has no state {#dd-combinational}

Extend the multiplier into the FMA used by the first exercise:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```systemverilog
wire [7:0] product;

assign product =
    {4'b0, a} * {4'b0, b};

assign d =
    {1'b0, product} + {5'b0, c};
```
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.incremental}
- The hardware contains a multiplier feeding an adder.

- Gates respond concurrently; the dependency creates a propagation path.

- Nothing is "executed" in source order.

- There is no clock or stored value. Width and signedness define the arithmetic.
:::
:::
::::

## Registers introduce state and clock cycles {#dd-registers}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```systemverilog
logic [7:0] product_q;
logic [8:0] c_q;

always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  product_q <= {4'b0, a} * {4'b0, b};
  c_q       <= {5'b0, c};
end

assign d = {1'b0, product_q} + c_q;
```
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.incremental}
- A register samples its input on a clock edge.

- Its output holds the sampled value until the next active edge.

- Combinational logic still propagates concurrently **between** registers.

- This register layer adds a cycle; throughput is a separate design choice.
:::
:::
::::

## Modules create hierarchy {#dd-hierarchy}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
```systemverilog
module fma4(
  input  logic [3:0] a, b, c,
  output logic [8:0] d
);
  logic [7:0] product;

  mul4 u_mul(
    .a(a), .b(b), .p(product));

  assign d =
      {1'b0, product} + {5'b0, c};
endmodule
```
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.incremental}
- A **module** defines a reusable boundary.

- An **instance** creates hardware.

- Ports connect signals across that boundary.

- Combinational and sequential logic may coexist inside it; the boundary itself
  adds no clock cycle.
:::
:::
::::

## An FPGA is a configurable circuit {#dd-fpga-analogy}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
![Left: a cellular automaton. Right: a simple FPGA. Adapted from [@popoff2026frugality].](assets/images/digital-design/fpga-cellular-automaton.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="A cellular automaton grid beside a simple FPGA grid with configurable cells and richer programmable interconnect" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
**Analogy:** an FPGA is to a cellular automaton what a CPU is to a Turing
machine.

::: {.incremental}
- A grid of configurable logic cells

- A programmable interconnection network

- Combinational paths **and** clocked state

- Manufactured once, configured for many circuits
:::
:::
::::

## A bitstream configures structure {#dd-fpga-configuration}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
![Left: a configurable logic cell containing a LUT and register. Right: one configured path through an FPGA. Adapted from [@popoff2026frugality].](assets/images/digital-design/fpga-lut-configured.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="A lookup-table cell with a one-bit register beside an FPGA fabric whose selected cells and routes are highlighted" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Configuration**

- Place and route the circuit.
- Set LUT tables, registers, and routing switches. A 4-input LUT needs
  $2^4=16$ bits.

::: {.fragment}
**Execution**

- Connections stay fixed.
- Signals propagate; registers sample on clock edges.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Bitstream:** circuit configuration, **not a CPU instruction stream**.
:::
:::
::::

## A modern FPGA is more than LUTs {#dd-fpga-resources}

| FPGA resource | Hardware role |
|---|---|
| LUT + register | Boolean logic and one bit of state |
| programmable routing | wires between resources |
| DSP block | hard multiplier or multiply-accumulate |
| block RAM | on-chip storage |
| I/O blocks | off-chip communication |
| CPU system on some devices | software, external memory, and peripherals |

::: {.fragment}
The same multiplier may become LUT logic or a hard DSP block. Mapping is a
target decision; the arithmetic semantics remain the same
[@popoff2026frugality].
:::

## An ASIC fixes the circuit in silicon {#dd-asic-cells}

An FPGA is configured after fabrication. An ASIC fixes one circuit during
fabrication. Even an OR gate becomes geometry:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="31%"}
**RTL**

```systemverilog
assign y = a | b;
```
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
![Logic schematic of a SKY130 OR2 standard cell. [@ledoux2024thesis]](assets/images/digital-design/sky130-or2-schematic.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Schematic representation of a two-input OR standard cell" width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="35%"}
![Physical layout of the same SKY130 OR2 cell. [@ledoux2024thesis]](assets/images/digital-design/sky130-or2-layout-cropped.svg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Colored GDSII geometry for a two-input OR standard cell" height="350"}
:::
::::

::: {.incremental}
- **Logic synthesis** decomposes the datapath and chooses library cells.

- **Place and route** assigns coordinates to every cell and wire.
:::

## An ASIC is placed and routed {#dd-asic-layout}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
![Placed-and-routed floating-point divider. [@ledoux2024thesis]](assets/images/digital-design/gds-divider.jpg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Physical-design view of a routed floating-point divider with standard cells, clock tree, power grid, and signal wires" height="560"}
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Cells occupy **area**.

- Wires have **length, delay, and congestion**.

- Clock and power need their own networks.

- The hardware description is becoming a physical object.
:::
:::
::::

## Hierarchy becomes floorplan {#dd-floorplan}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="63%"}
![Labelled Intel Core i9-13900K die shot. JmsDoug and Fritzchens Fritz, CC0.](assets/images/intel-i9-13900k-labelled-die.jpg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Labelled Intel Core i9-13900K die showing processor cores, cache arrays, interconnect, graphics, media engines, and I/O logic" height="560"}
:::

::: {.column width="37%"}
At chip scale, hierarchy is no longer only a name in the RTL.

::: {.incremental}
- Instances repeat hardware.

- Large modules and memories become visible regions.

- Floorplanning assigns those regions coordinates.

- The description has become **geometry**.
:::
:::
::::

## These concepts need compiler vocabulary {#dd-vocabulary}

| Digital-design concept | Question made explicit |
|---|---|
| combinational dataflow, width, signedness | what exists between state elements? |
| register and clock | what is stored, and at which cycle boundary? |
| module, instance, port | what hardware exists, and how is it connected? |
| FSM, mux, enable | how is the next state selected? |
| memory, stream, protocol | where does data live, and how does it move? |
| cell, wire, floorplan | where and in which technology will it exist? |

::: {.fragment}
We started with one multiplication. It became concurrent logic, state,
hierarchy, cells, wires, and geometry. **CIRCT gives those decisions distinct
MLIR representations.**
:::
